analysis.one_liner: Requires car companies to get your permission before selling your driving and location data.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in late September 2024 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it died with no hearing, no vote, and no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for car makers, insurers, and app companies to sell or share data collected from your car — where you drove, how you drove, where the car is parked — unless you first got a plain-language notice and explicitly said yes. You could take that permission back at any time through a website, app, or the mail. It would also force car makers and insurers to report their data practices to the Federal Trade Commission every year, and direct the FTC to write rules for how car makers handle location tracking in domestic violence situations. Violations would be enforced by the FTC like other unfair or deceptive business practices.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who drives a car — or rides in one. Connected cars today collect precise location and driving-behavior data that has been sold to data brokers and insurers, sometimes raising people's insurance premiums based on driving habits they never agreed to share. The bill would flip the default: no sale or sharing of that data without your explicit, revocable consent. It would also give domestic violence survivors a rules framework for situations where an abuser can track a car's location through a manufacturer's app.

how_it_helps.text: Requires car makers, insurers, and data-collecting app companies to provide a clear, standalone notice and get affirmative express consent before selling or sharing any consumer car-related data, including precise location and driving history [S2].
Consent cannot be buried in a terms-of-service agreement or obtained through misleading means, and consumers can revoke it at any time through the company's website, app, or by mail [S2].

Requires every car manufacturer and motor vehicle insurance company to report annually to the FTC on what car data they collect, why, and who they share or sell it to, with the FTC publishing a yearly summary to Congress [S2].

Directs the FTC, with the FCC and highway safety regulators, to issue guidance or rules within 180 days on how car makers should address domestic violence risks tied to apps that can pinpoint a car's location [S2].
Enforces the law through the Federal Trade Commission's existing unfair-and-deceptive-practices authority, with rulemaking power to fill in the details [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Car manufacturers, auto insurers, telematics companies, and data brokers that profit from collecting and reselling car and driving data would lose that revenue stream and face new reporting and compliance duties. Some connected-car services that depend on data sharing — for example, insurance discounts based on driving monitoring — would require an explicit opt-in and might reach fewer customers.

drawbacks.text: An opt-in requirement is stricter than most current state privacy laws, and it would apply to sharing with any company, not just sales to third parties; some services drivers find useful, such as accident-response or usage-based insurance discounts, would need a separate explicit sign-up and could reach fewer people [S2].

The bill's only sharing exception is for the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration; it does not address sharing with police, courts, or other government bodies, leaving a gap the rulemaking would have to work around [S2].
Compliance costs — annual privacy reports to the FTC and new consent systems — would fall on manufacturers and insurers, costs that could partly be passed to consumers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but modest on the cost side: drivers give up one-click默认 data sharing in exchange for control over highly sensitive location and driving data, which has documented links to insurance rate increases. The strictness of the opt-in model is a genuine design debate, but the bill's transparency reports and domestic-violence guidance address real harms. On balance the benefits to ordinary drivers outweigh the compliance burden.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in September 2024, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on September 25, 2024, joined by Sen. Elizabeth Warren; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S4].
The bill had 2 cosponsors, both Democrats [S3].
No further action was taken — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action appears in the bill's history before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers, auto insurers, and the data-broker industry that buys and resells car and driving data came out ahead, because they keep collecting and selling that data without needing explicit consent. Drivers gained nothing, since the bill never advanced beyond a committee referral.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Car makers, insurers, and data brokers

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Car Privacy Rights Act and referred it to the Commerce Committee.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress [S4].

sides.party_line_note: The bill's three Senate supporters were all Democrats, and with only 2 cosponsors it never attracted any Republican backing [S3].

industries.note: Connected-car programs collect precise location and driving-behavior data that manufacturers have sold or shared with third parties; the bill would require explicit consent before any sharing, cutting off that revenue and forcing annual disclosure of their data practices [S2]. Drivers' interest in keeping their location private runs directly against this business line.

Insurers buy driving-behavior data to set rates, and some have raised premiums based on data drivers never knowingly shared; the bill requires their explicit consent for such data and subjects them to annual reporting [S2]. Insurers lose a data channel; drivers could see fairer premiums.

Companies that aggregate and resell car location and driving data would lose their supply unless each consumer opts in [S2]. Their profit comes from selling information about people who never agreed to the sale.
The bill hands the FTC new enforcement jurisdiction, annual industry reporting, and rulemaking duties over car data privacy [S2].
